Graph neural networks (GNNs) have proven highly effective for graph representation learning, yet their application to graph retrieval remains underexplored. This study introduces a novel model designed for graph retrieval, aligning models at the node and edge levels to identify shared structural patterns. We evaluate this approach on a real-world graph retrieval scenario involving the identification of similar supply chain networks. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms baseline approaches, achieving superior retrieval quality.

We introduce a methodology for capturing transient dynamics within a system by leveraging a trained language model. Our approach involves treating time-series data as sequences of discrete tokens, which are then processed and fine-tuned using Natural Language Processing (NLP) strategies. We demonstrate that this method significantly enhances the ability to capture transient dynamics, particularly in regimes where traditional machine learning models fail.

This study examines the allocation of divisible resources, such as electricity, among a group of consumers. We introduce a new method for distributing these resources that adheres to both efficiency and fairness principles. Specifically, we demonstrate that our algorithm achieves Pareto optimality, envy-freeness, and proportionality. Furthermore, we prove that the mechanism requires only logarithmic time to compute, making it efficient for practical implementation.

Event coreference identification (ECI) involves locating references to the same event within a collection of news documents. This paper introduces a dataset specifically designed for the controversial political domain, along with a baseline system that achieves an F1 score of 73.3% on this data. The study also demonstrates that current state-of-the-art models struggle with this domain, primarily due to their training data being heavily skewed toward non-political content.

The Complementarity Knapsack Problem (CKP) is an application of the more comprehensive Complementarity Problem (CP), which seeks to determine a vector $x$ satisfying the condition that $x \geq 0$ and the inequality $f(x) \geq 0$ hold alongside the constraint $x^T f(x) = 0$. This study examines CKP instances where $f(x) = Ax + b$, with $A$ defined as a matrix and $b$ as a vector. We demonstrate that the facets of the feasible region associated with CKP can be organized into distinct categories. Furthermore, we provide a method for enumerating these facet categories and establish sufficient conditions under which the face of the feasible region can be fully characterized by a specific subset of these categories.

This paper introduces the notion of generalized $(m,n)$-Jordan derivation and investigates its characteristics within modules, after which it examines how normalizers relate to these derivations in finite-dimensional algebras. Additionally, it demonstrates that every such derivation, in the context of prime rings, amounts to a linear combination of an inner generalized derivation and a linear component.
We demonstrate that the 2-factor emerging in Weinberg's soft graviton theorem originates from the constraints of the spin-2 field.

We define transversal groups within the context of nonlinear projection operators acting on vector-valued functions, utilizing this framework to establish a sharp bound regarding the Hausdorff dimension of the images derived from polynomial curves under such nonlinear projections.

We introduce a directed search algorithm for reinforcement learning that utilizes minimal human demonstrations to achieve control performance comparable to model predictive control (MPC). Unlike traditional approaches, our method does not require a model of the environment's dynamics. We observe that tube MPC, which employs robust techniques to handle uncertainty, can be recast as a robust bilevel program. This reformulation enables the use of directed policy search to learn an efficient policy from a limited set of demonstrations. We validate this approach on a simulation of a quadrotor, where it successfully tracks dynamic trajectories with high accuracy despite being trained on just a single demonstration.

We introduce a generalized semiclassical framework for analyzing the Hall effect in noncentrosymmetric systems, which accommodates arbitrary magnetic fields and crystal orientations. This approach enables a comprehensive investigation of the intrinsic Hall effect in the cubic regime, where the third-order conductivity tensor exhibits a unique symmetry. We determine the analytical expressions for the Hall conductivity as a function of orientation relative to the cubic axes and map out the corresponding dispersion relations for Hall edge states. Our findings indicate that the third-order intrinsic Hall effect is robust against variations in crystal orientation, distinguishing it from the conventional Hall effect, which is highly sensitive to orientation.

We introduce a method for creating call graph representations that are invariant to reordering, enabling pairwise comparisons to generate embeddings suitable for clustering and dimensionality reduction. This framework facilitates the analysis of call graph similarities across multiple programs, revealing patterns in their interactions and identifying groups with shared characteristics. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness and scalability by applying it to a dataset of 100,000 C programs, each containing an average of 100 functions.

The One Billion Word Benchmark (OWB) has served as a standard metric for evaluating word embeddings, with top performance defined by the ability to retrieve the correct target word from a pool of distractors. This study examines the underlying assumptions of this evaluation method, demonstrating that the inherent noise in the dataset can render benchmark results misleading. Specifically, we show that the One Billion Word Continuous Word Evaluation (OWCE) metric is susceptible to data contamination, allowing high-performing models to achieve top rankings even when they rely on trivial or spurious correlations rather than genuine semantic understanding. Our findings indicate that the noise level in the dataset is substantial enough to undermine the validity of current assessments.

Quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) are a common feature in solar flares, yet their physical origins remain uncertain. This study investigates a specific flare event on 2014 March 29, which exhibited a prominent QPO in microwave emissions. By analyzing microwave data from the Nobeyama Radioheliograph and X-ray data from the Reuven Ramaty High-Energy Solar Spectroscopic Explorer, we identified a QPO with a period of 10.5 minutes in both microwave and X-ray bands. This oscillation was observed in microwave emissions from the flare's footpoints and in X-ray emissions from the loop top. We propose that the microwave emissions arise from the gyro-synchrotron mechanism, while the X-ray emissions result from thermal bremsstrahlung. Our findings suggest that the QPO originates in the flare's current sheet, driven by the periodic formation of magnetic islands through the tearing mode instability.

Anomaly detection is a critical component of industrial quality control, yet existing methods often struggle with the high variability of real-world manufacturing environments. To address this, we introduce a novel approach for anomaly detection that leverages multi-scale features and the Contrario framework. The method begins by extracting multi-scale features from images using a pre-trained ResNet model, followed by identifying anomalies through the Contrario mechanism. Experimental results indicate that this approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating robustness across various industrial scenarios.

This paper investigates the dispersion-generalized Kadomtsev-Petviashvili I (KP-I) equation, defined by $\partial_t u+u_{xxx}+\alpha u_{tt}+\beta u_{y}u_{yy}+\alpha u_{xxx}+\partial_x(u^3)+u_{xxx}+\alpha u_{tt}+\beta u_{yy}u+\partial_x(u^3)=0$ (where $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}$). We establish well-posedness for this dispersion-generalized KP-I in irregular Sobolev spaces $H^s(\mathbb{R}^2)$ under the condition $s\geq \frac{3}{2}\alpha-\frac{3}{2}$. This threshold represents the most significant irregularity for which we can achieve well-posedness, as it aligns with the bilinear resonance. Our approach relies on the bilinear $L^2(L^2)$ estimate alongside the method of energy estimates.

We investigate the Kramers degeneracy within open quantum systems, specifically focusing on how degeneracy points are affected when parity-time ($\mathcal{PT}$) symmetry is broken. Our findings indicate that these critical degeneracy points are robustly preserved even under non-Hermitian conditions, a property that remains valid regardless of whether the system is in the $\mathcal{PT}$-broken phase. This preservation is further confirmed by the fact that the eigenstates corresponding to degenerate points are always real, a characteristic that holds true in the $\mathcal{PT}$-broken regime.

This study introduces a new approach for downlink precoding in high-mobility massive MIMO systems, which leverages the temporal correlation of channel state information (CSI) to predict future channel responses. By utilizing a deep neural network (DNN) to model the non-linear relationship between successive CSI samples, the method anticipates downstream CSI requirements. Simulation results demonstrate that this prediction capability allows for the reuse of previously acquired CSI data, thereby reducing the frequency of pilot transmissions and enhancing overall system efficiency.

This study addresses the challenge of estimating the true minor region within a stochastic binary sequence by utilizing a disparity measure defined as the count of ones preceding the initial zero. We propose a Bayesian estimation framework employing a mixture of Beta distributions to model the prior distribution of this measure. The primary contribution involves a novel, computationally efficient algorithm for inferring the posterior distribution of this measure, which relies on the prior's mixture structure and avoids the need for costly Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling. We further demonstrate that the estimated minor region converges in probability toward the true minor region as the sequence length approaches infinity.

This work investigates the asymptotic behavior of Szeg\H{o} polynomials defined on complex hypoelliptic contact structures, specifically Grauert tubes, which are constructed from Riemannian manifolds. We demonstrate that as the degree of the Szeg\H{o} polynomials increases, their behavior converges to that of the standard model on the Heisenberg group. Furthermore, we establish a uniform bound for the derivatives of the Szeg\H{o} functions, with growth rates that are consistent with the model's asymptotics. These findings are derived from a detailed examination of the Grauert tube's contact geometry and the associated Heisenberg calculus.

The reverse line chart creation task involves determining a sequence of positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ given a list of $n$ values representing the cumulative sum of their prefix sums. This study examines two distinct approaches for solving this problem: Roussopoulos's method and the MARINLINGA algorithm. Both techniques successfully address the challenge in polynomial time, with MARINLINGA offering superior efficiency by requiring only $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space, whereas Roussopoulos's method operates within $O(n^2)$ time complexity and utilizes $O(n)$ space.
This paper demonstrates that the conjecture Lee and Lee proposed regarding rigid modules over a local ring, which they termed a "hypothesis," is correct.

The Java ecosystem has grown into a vast network of interlinked libraries, with developers frequently relying on tools to manage this complexity. Despite this, the long-term effects of library dependencies on code quality remain poorly understood. This study examines the impact of such dependencies on the stability, performance, and defect rates of Java software. We analyzed 1,000 open-source Java projects from the 2016 Eclipse Sonatype Code Analysis dataset, focusing on those with substantial dependency graphs. Our findings indicate that projects with more dependencies are significantly more prone to failures, experience greater runtime overhead, and suffer degraded performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate that developers often inflate dependencies unnecessarily, complicating the maintenance of their code. We conclude by offering practical recommendations to mitigate these challenges.

We examine the entanglement of biphoton-regulated synthesis within a sequence of $N$ coupled chains, where every pair of adjacent chains shares entanglement. We demonstrate that this system exhibits a kinship effect, characterized by the rapid convergence of the final chain's state to the initial chain's state as $N$ increases. This phenomenon is driven by the exponential decay of the probability that a photon travels backward through the chain, a pattern that aligns with findings from prior research. We further explore how increasing the degree of biphotonal entanglement influences the chain's evolution. Additionally, we analyze the impact of incorporating a rival chain, which disrupts the kinship effect by inducing significant rivalry.

This study examines multistage distributionally resilient optimization (MDRO) within a robust representation of multistage stochastic linear programs (MSLPs). In this framework, uncertainty is modeled via a set of probability measures, and the objective is to minimize expected costs across all potential probability scenarios. The authors introduce a new MDRO model that incorporates a total variation (TV) distance constraint to limit the difference between any feasible solution's probability and a reference probability. This approach offers a more robust and conservative solution compared to traditional MDRO formulations. The research demonstrates that the proposed MDRO model is a linear program with a variable count that remains independent of the number of uncertainty scenarios. Furthermore, the study provides a closed-form expression for the optimal value function of the MDRO problem, proving that it is piecewise linear and convex with respect to the reference probability distribution.

This study introduces a new recurrent neural network (RNN) framework designed for action prediction, which employs radial basis function (RBF) kernels to map input features. The core objective is to enhance the model's capacity to capture non-linear relationships between input features and future actions. We demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in this domain. Furthermore, we validate the model's efficacy in predicting both human and robot actions.

We introduce a new deep thermalization framework that employs a sequence of unitary gates to drive quantum systems into their thermal states. This approach utilizes a distinct set of design times for every gate, allowing for the creation of a unified, solvable theoretical model. We establish a rigorous mathematical proof demonstrating that this framework successfully achieves deep thermalization, supported by numerical simulations that confirm the method's practical effectiveness.

This study establishes the necessary and sufficient conditions for a symbol $a(x,\xi)$ defined on a uniform tree to belong to a bounded pseudo-differential operator $B(\Lambda^n)$ within a specific Besov-type Besov space $B^s_{p,q}(\Lambda^n)$. Furthermore, we investigate the nuclearity criteria for these operators and demonstrate that they form a nuclear class under specific parameter constraints.

The proliferation of smartphones has driven the creation of specialized mobile networks designed to handle their unique requirements. This paper examines the visibility of smartphones within 5G environments, specifically focusing on the device's ability to detect and connect to visible 5G base stations. We introduce a novel dataset comprising 1,000 measurements taken across diverse 5G scenarios, where visibility is determined by the device's 5G radio connectivity. Our analysis reveals that smartphone visibility in 5G networks is significantly higher than in 4G networks, with an average detection rate of 94.4% compared to 73.2% in 4G. Furthermore, we observe that visibility is primarily influenced by the device's distance from the base station and the surrounding urban environment.

Contemporary deep learning models often exhibit excessive confidence when processing out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs, a flaw that can lead to severe real-world consequences. This paper introduces the Chamfer Out-of-Distribution (CODE) dataset, a novel collection of OOD samples designed specifically to evaluate deep neural networks. Unlike prior OOD datasets, the samples in the Chamfer OOD dataset are not generated by manipulating existing images; instead, they are entirely synthesized using a diffusion model. This study presents the first measurement of azimuthal correlations for 2-jet, 3-jet, and 4-jet events in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The analysis utilizes data from the CMS detector at the CERN LHC, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 19.6 fb$^{-1}$. The correlation coefficients for the transverse momenta of the constituent jets are determined using the angle between the CMS forward calorimeter and the jet plane. The observed data are compared to predictions from Monte Carlo event generators, including PYTHIA8, HERWIG++, and ALPGEN, as well as parton shower simulations from HERWIG++ and parton-level calculations from HERWIG++. The results indicate that PYTHIA8 and HERWIG++ provide the most accurate descriptions of the 2-jet and 3-jet correlation coefficients, whereas ALPGEN and parton-level HERWIG++ models are better suited for 4-jet correlations.

The surge in accessible visual data has driven the need for advanced algorithms to extract meaningful insights. While deep learning has proven highly effective in computer vision, its application is often hindered by the scarcity of labeled data. To address this, researchers have developed semi-supervised and unsupervised learning strategies, which have yielded significant results in the visual education domain. This paper reviews recent developments in these techniques, specifically focusing on their use with visual education datasets. We examine the primary methodologies and categorize existing studies into unsupervised and semi-supervised frameworks, providing a comprehensive overview of current advancements in deep visual education.

Detecting outliers is a fundamental challenge in machine learning, with applications spanning anomaly detection, data cleaning, and recommendation systems. While numerous algorithms exist for this purpose, most rely on complex, opaque models that obscure the underlying reasons for identifying specific instances as anomalies. This paper introduces RECol, a straightforward and efficient method for outlier detection that leverages reconstruction error. By utilizing a pre-trained generative model, RECol assesses an outlier candidate based on the difficulty the model faces in reconstructing the point. We demonstrate that RECol is versatile, applicable to various generative models and domains, and capable of performing well without requiring additional training. Furthermore, we show that it surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in both efficiency and effectiveness.

This study examines the uniformity of the solution for non-linear Young equations, defined as $f(x)=x+\int_0^xf(f^2)\,dx$. We establish that the solution is uniformly continuous in the space of bounded variation. This continuity is shown to be equivalent to the space of bounded variation being isomorphic to the space of bounded functions under the supremum norm. This result is applied to demonstrate that the solution of rough differential equations driven by functions in the space of bounded variation is also uniformly continuous. This finding is significant because it establishes a form of robustness for the solution with respect to small perturbations in the underlying function.

We introduce an enhanced methodology for determining the neutrino polarizability, a parameter that encapsulates potential new physics within the Standard Model. Our approach utilizes the electroweak scattering of neutrinos off longitudinally polarized electrons, demonstrating that it achieves superior precision compared to previous techniques involving neutrino-electron scattering and neutrino pair production off muons.

This study examines the emergence of rhythmic behavior in a mean field model of a neuron-glial system. The model incorporates a neuron described by a two-dimensional generalized FitzHugh-Nagumo equation coupled with a third-variable cell governed by a first-order ordinary differential equation. We demonstrate that the system can display limit cycle behavior, which is absent in either the individual neuron or glial components. Furthermore, we identify the specific parameter ranges responsible for this oscillation and analyze how the coupling strength influences the system's dynamics.

This study examines the quantum behavior of a neutral spin-1/2 particle within a specific magnetic field configuration. The field is constructed to generate a uniform force along the z-axis, counterbalanced by a magnetic field gradient oriented along the same axis. Under these conditions, the particle's wave function evolves according to a Dirac equation that lacks explicit dependence on the z-coordinate. We demonstrate that the resulting solutions to this Dirac equation possess both abelian and non-abelian topological attributes. Furthermore, we establish that the associated topological characteristics are governed by the background field parameters.

We introduce a novel mechanism for boundary erosion in growing clusters, termed the initial-passage-driven (IPD) mechanism. This process occurs when a random walker, who has already visited a site, later encounters it again via a different path, causing its removal. Consequently, the cluster boundary undergoes erosion whenever such a distinct return route exists. The IPD mechanism is particularly significant for clusters with fractal characteristics, where the initial-passage probability scales as $p_{\rm{I}}(s) \sim s^{-\alpha}$ with $\alpha < 1$. We demonstrate that the fractal dimension $d_{\rm{f}}$ of a cluster is determined by $\alpha$ and the spatial dimension $d$ through the relation $d_{\rm{f}} = (d + \alpha - 1)/(d - \alpha)$. By applying this framework to various growth models, we establish that the IPD mechanism is a universal feature of cluster growth.

We introduce a novel method for calculating hyperbolic L-space links by integrating satellite link theory with the analysis of L-graphs. This synthesis enables the identification of an expansive family of hyperbolic L-space links. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these families possess infinitely many distinct knots that share the same hyperbolic volume.

We investigate the kinetic theory of Brownian particles in a disorder field, specifically examining the hydrodynamic limit as the number of particles approaches infinity while the disorder's spatial scale shrinks to zero. By demonstrating that the resulting hydrodynamic limit equations remain invariant under a certain Poisson structure, we establish a covariant mapping between the kinetic and hydrodynamic frameworks. This approach offers a novel perspective on kinetic theory and provides an exact covariant bridge connecting the Vlasov-Poisson system with Euler's equations, distinct from standard weak solutions which rely on approximating the Coulomb interaction via a smooth kernel.

This study introduces a novel framework for automatically identifying surgical artifacts within endoscopic footage. The approach integrates two distinct components: an endoscopic video processing pipeline and an object detection system. The video processing stage handles the initial extraction of surgical artifacts from the endoscopic feed, while the detection system evaluates the reliability of this extraction. The detection framework is built upon a library of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained to recognize surgical artifacts. The two modules function together in an iterative loop, where the processing component refines its output based on reliability scores generated by the detection component. The entire system was validated using a dataset of 1,000 endoscopic video clips from laparoscopic cholecystectomies, annotated with surgical artifacts. The results indicate that the iterative process significantly boosts the system's accuracy, raising the F1 score from 0.71 to 0.81.

This study examines the formation and meaning of syntactic patterns within identifier names in source code, specifically addressing how developers construct these names and the insights they provide regarding code semantics. We introduce a novel methodology for automatically detecting these patterns, which integrates techniques from pattern mining, information theory, and natural language processing. By applying this approach to three distinct programming languages, we demonstrate that syntax patterns are not merely arbitrary but are deeply rooted in the specific domain and code context. Furthermore, we illustrate how these patterns can be leveraged to enhance code search capabilities.

Human pose estimation (HPE) and human shape estimation (HSE) are foundational to numerous computer vision applications, including augmented reality, human-computer interaction, and computer graphics. While recent advancements have yielded highly accurate algorithms, a critical gap remains: a comprehensive evaluation of these methods across diverse real-world scenarios. This study addresses that gap by conducting a systematic assessment of state-of-the-art HPE and HSE techniques using a broad spectrum of real-world datasets. We introduce a novel framework designed to analyze and compare these algorithms, examining the influence of various factors such as dataset characteristics, model architectures, and input modalities. Our findings reveal that current methods often fail to perform reliably in real-world conditions, with results varying significantly based on the specific input type employed.

We investigate the superconducting properties of a two-dimensional lattice of weakly interacting quantum dots, where interdot tunneling is mediated by conduction electrons. In this system, the effective interaction between electrons is driven by the exchange of even numbers of auxiliary conduction electrons. We demonstrate that this interaction can become sufficiently strong to trigger superconductivity. Furthermore, we analyze the system's ground state in the limit of strong electron-electron coupling, showing that it resembles a BCS state.

We examine the matching of a four-fermion operator framework to a theory featuring scalar leptoquarks at a lepton-quark interaction vertex. The study covers both left- and right-handed scenarios, as well as both product forms of four-fermion operators. We establish the matching coefficients for lepton and distinct quark flavors at zero matching scale, and subsequently determine the renormalization group evolution of these four-fermion operators from the matching scale down to the electroweak scale.

This paper presents a novel classification theory for machine learning, establishing a conceptual framework for analyzing classification performance. It demonstrates that classification accuracy is bound by an inherent limit, which the study seeks to maximize. Consequently, an optimal classification theory is formulated to optimize model performance, a theoretical approach that also guides the design of superior machine learning models.

The proposed sliding-mode control function is defined by ideal sliding conditions, ensuring that system trajectories converge to the sliding manifold within a finite time interval. The designed sliding-mode algorithm guarantees that the sliding motion proceeds ideally, eliminating the sliding-mode phenomenon. Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are integral to modern technology, yet their internal architecture remains largely hidden to researchers. This study introduces a non-destructive, quantitative method to determine the layered internal structure of LIBs by utilizing low-frequency ultrasonic waves. The technique relies on the distinct acoustic responses of various components within the cell. By analyzing the reflected ultrasonic signals, we successfully identified the individual layers of the battery stack. The method's efficacy was validated using a 20Ah pouch cell, and the resulting layer characterization was corroborated against data from X-ray computed tomography (CT) scans.

This paper introduces a discrete-time flatness-based control method for the swing-up and stabilization tasks of gantry cranes. The approach involves deriving a discrete-time model by discretizing the continuous gantry crane dynamics, followed by applying flatness-based control to manage the system. The study demonstrates that this strategy ensures convergence of gantry crane dynamics to the desired equilibrium point, with the proposed control scheme validated through numerical simulations.

Image captioning involves generating textual descriptions that explain the content of an image. A primary challenge in this field is the scarcity of large-scale datasets containing manually annotated captions, which are both expensive and time-intensive to create. To address this, researchers have developed methods that leverage noisy, automatically generated captions—such as those produced by machine learning models—to augment training data. However, the inclusion of inaccurate pseudo-labels can significantly degrade model performance. This paper introduces a cooperative distillation framework designed to mitigate the adverse effects of noisy data. Our approach utilizes the complementary information between visual features and textual outputs to enhance the training process. Specifically, we propose a method for estimating the reliability of generated pseudo-labels, which is then integrated into the distillation objective to reduce their detrimental impact. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques on three established benchmark datasets.

We demonstrate that for any $k \geq 1$ and any $k$-tuple of positive integers $(n_1, \dots, n_k)$, there exists an integer $N$ such that every set $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ containing at least $|S|/2$ distinct residue classes modulo $n_i$ for each $i$ must house a monochromatic arithmetic progression of length $k$ with common difference at least $N$. This outcome extends a prior finding by Pham and Vu regarding binary sequences. Furthermore, we establish that such an AP of length $k$ can be found with difference $d \geq N^\epsilon$ for any fixed $\epsilon > 0$, provided $|S|/2$ is substituted with the threshold $(1-\epsilon)n/2$.

We introduce the notion of an arranged Ehresmann semigroup and present an arithmetical formula for its right regularity. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between the category of arranged Ehresmann semigroups and ordered topological categories with specific properties, as well as an equivalence to an alternative category defined through equivalent characteristics.

Self-attention mechanisms have become a cornerstone of modern natural language processing, with their efficacy in transformer architectures heavily influenced by design choices regarding depth and width. This study investigates how self-attention performance varies with these parameters, specifically examining the interaction between depth and width. We demonstrate that while shallow attention layers can theoretically match the expressive power of deep ones, they fail to do so in practice. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel framework called "depth-width coupled self-attention," which integrates both parameters to enhance expressive capabilities. Experimental results indicate that our method outperforms existing approaches in both language modeling and machine translation tasks.

This study details the synthesis of BiFeO$_3$ nanoparticles using a sol-gel method at a low temperature of 300°C. The resulting nanomaterials were characterized via XRD, SEM, TEM, and UV-Vis spectroscopy, with their magnetic properties analyzed through VSM. The material exhibits a room-temperature magnetization of 0.11 emu/g, alongside a band gap of 2.5 eV. Furthermore, the nanoparticles demonstrate significant photocatalytic efficiency in hydrogen generation and the degradation of methylene blue dye. These findings underscore the potential of BiFeO$_3$ nanoparticles as effective, low-cost, and sustainable agents for environmental applications.

We examine a toy ${\rm SU}(6)$ model that generates masses for the first generation of matter quarks and leptons, specifically the bottom quark and tau lepton, through Yukawa couplings. The mass ratios for these particles are governed by the product of two parameters: a Yukawa coupling and a triplet mass. We demonstrate that the model successfully reproduces the observed mass ratios of the bottom quark and tau particle, along with their respective mixing angles, provided the mass of the triplet particle is approximately $10^{16}$ GeV.

We introduce a novel approach to the 3D reconstruction of generic objects held in hands, a task that is notoriously difficult due to the complex interplay between the item and the hand, which significantly distorts the item's visual appearance. To address this, we propose a new method that jointly reconstructs the 3D shape of the item and the hand simultaneously. By leveraging the fact that held objects typically resemble known 3D categories, we utilize a pre-trained 3D shape prior to guide the reconstruction process. Our method employs a network that takes a single RGB image as input and produces a 3D object representation by optimizing a differentiable rendering loss. This loss function is computed by comparing the synthesized image of the predicted 3D hand and object against the original input. Our results demonstrate that this approach successfully reconstructs the 3D shape of the item and the hand together, effectively overcoming the visual distortions caused by the grasping action.

The Ca-K index, a widely used metric for monitoring solar activity, is a composite of absorption and reversal lines within the K I doublet at 7664.6 and 7669.92 Å. This study analyzes a century-long dataset of equal-contrast images from Kodaikanal Observatory to examine variations in the Ca-K index and its characteristics. The research reveals that the Ca-K index undergoes significant modification due to changes in atmospheric conditions, specifically cloud cover and humidity. Furthermore, the study finds that the index is more sensitive to cloud cover during periods of high solar activity.

The $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay represents a rare process with a branching fraction of approximately $10^{-8}$, serving as a valuable probe for new physics beyond the Standard Model. This study presents a proof of this decay mode using data from LHCb, derived from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 1.0 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis identified 11 candidate events, yielding a signal significance of 4.4 standard deviations.

Test-depth segmentation serves as a pivotal technique for symbolically analyzing the control of hybrid systems. This approach involves partitioning the state space into segments where the system's discrete mode remains constant. This paper introduces an algorithm for distributed test-depth segmentation applicable to linear hybrid systems. The method proceeds in two stages: first, it distributes the computation of candidate segments across distributed nodes, and second, it consolidates these results by eliminating redundant segments and resolving conflicts at the boundaries between adjacent continuous modes. We demonstrate the algorithm's efficacy through its application to a linear hybrid system used in a distributed missile guidance context.

We investigate the magnetization reversal of a square-lattice chain composed of magnetic nanoparticles, where each element is modeled as a spin with magnitude $S=10$ and coupled via exchange interactions. The system's behavior is governed by two dimensionless parameters: the ratio of inter-particle exchange coupling to the single-particle anisotropy, and the external magnetic field strength. We identify a specific region in the phase diagram where the system exhibits a rejuvenation phenomenon. This process involves a sequence of two first-order magnetization transitions; the second transition occurs only after cooling the system below a critical temperature $T_c$ following an initial magnetization under a strong field. This finding aligns with earlier studies on single-spin clusters but extends the concept to systems with inter-spin exchange interactions.

Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising approach for distributed machine learning, yet its performance is often hindered by the scarcity of labeled data and the risk of malicious clients. This paper introduces a novel FL framework designed to overcome these obstacles by leveraging social networks. By utilizing the social structure, the proposed method enables clients to establish trust relationships with verified neighbors, thereby mitigating the data scarcity issue. Simultaneously, it implements a hub-free architecture to prevent single points of failure and vulnerability to adversarial attacks. The study also presents a new social graph-based trust propagation algorithm that allows clients to identify reliable partners even when starting with limited labeled data. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that the proposed FL framework achieves superior accuracy compared to existing methods, while maintaining robustness against malicious clients.

This study presents a sequential categorization framework for short-text inputs, designed to capture both local and global contextual features. We employ hybrid Convolutional and Recurrent Neural Networks, where convolutional layers extract local features and recurrent units model the sequential dependencies inherent in short-text sequences. Experimental results indicate that our approach outperforms traditional text classification methods, such as TF-IDF, Naive Bayes, and Support Vector Machines, as well as other neural architectures like standalone CNNs, RNNs, and hybrid CNN-LNN models.

Fabry-P\'erot resonators are fundamental to many optical systems, including lasers, spectrometers, and interferometers. This study introduces a new analytical framework designed to determine the transmission and reflection coefficients of etalon-based devices configured in a telecentric arrangement. This telecentric setup ensures that the angle of incidence remains constant across the entire beam profile. The proposed method is applicable to any resonator featuring a constant optical path length for all beam components, regardless of incidence angle. By deriving the path length as a function of incidence angle, we establish a general formula for the transmission and reflection coefficients, which is subsequently applied to telecentric resonators. Specifically, we analyze two telecentric configurations: one comprising two flat surfaces and another consisting of two concentic spherical surfaces. Additionally, we examine the transmission characteristics of a telecentric resonator formed by two concentic spherical surfaces, demonstrating that the transmission coefficient is independent of the beam's radial position.

This study investigates the properties of pairings that remain invariant under the action of a group $G$. We establish that the pairing $B$ on a vector space $V$ and the pairing $B'$ on a vector space V' are compatible with the group $G$ if and only if $B'$ is equivalent to $B$ under a change of basis that commutes with the action of $G$. We also present examples illustrating how such compatible pairs can arise in natural settings.

This paper presents chiplet architecture as a compelling hardware design methodology, offering a flexible approach to constructing complex integrated circuits by integrating multiple smaller, independent dies. Chiplets significantly enhance design agility, shorten time-to-market, and reduce costs, while also improving yield and reliability. To fully leverage these advantages, chiplet-based systems require a robust framework for the efficient development of diverse, heterogeneous applications. We propose codelets as a modular, hardware-agnostic abstraction that encapsulates the fundamental components of these systems. By utilizing codelets, application developers can create modular, composable code that maps directly onto the hardware, enabling the construction of complex applications from simple, reusable units. We illustrate this approach through a series of examples, including the implementation of various algorithms and machine learning models using codelets.

Mixture cure models are frequently employed to analyze survival data within a population where a subset of individuals is already cured. In this study, we introduce a semiparametric framework that incorporates covariates into the mixture model, allowing these covariates to influence both the recurrence probability and the time-to-event distribution among the recurrent subgroup. We develop a method leveraging the presmoothing technique to estimate the parameters of this semiparametric formulation. Theoretical findings establish the asymptotic normality of the proposed estimator and the associated convergence rate. Furthermore, a simulation study is conducted to evaluate the method's performance. Finally, the approach is applied to a real dataset concerning the survival of patients with non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

We define the nonlocal distance dimension of a graph $G$ as the smallest cardinality of a subset $W \subseteq V(G)$ such that the sum of distances from any vertex $v \in V(G)$ to all vertices in $W$ uniquely identifies $v$. We establish that this nonlocal dimension is equivalent to the nonlocal metric dimension of the associated metric closure. Furthermore, we provide an algorithm capable of calculating this dimension for any given graph in polynomial time.

In-memory computing (IMC) has recently gained significant traction as a promising approach to overcome the limitations of conventional von Neumann architectures. However, this emerging technology introduces fresh security challenges, notably through potential side-channel attacks that exploit the processing framework. This paper investigates the security implications of IMC by analyzing two primary leakage models: leakage derived from power consumption and that originating from electromagnetic (EM) emissions. We propose a methodology to quantify the information leakage associated with IMC operations and validate it through empirical experiments. Our findings indicate that, under specific conditions, an adversary could successfully deduce the data being processed by observing EM emissions.

We introduce a framework utilizing polarization kernels to analyze the polarimetric properties of arbitrary polarization states. This approach decomposes any arbitrary state into two orthogonal components featuring distinct polarizations. By applying a kernel derived from the Stokes parameters of one of these basis vectors, the kernel effectively characterizes the state's polarization. This work derives the analytical expressions for these kernels and evaluates their behavior across various states. Furthermore, we examine how the kernel facilitates the calculation of polarized energy and entropy, with a specific focus on its application to polarization entanglement within quantum systems.

Seismic data is frequently compromised by blind-spot noise, such as surface waves, which obscure valuable information and hinder the quality of seismic images. While blind-spot deconvolution methods have been developed to address this, they often rely on supervised learning, which is constrained by the availability of clean training data. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a transfer learning strategy that utilizes self-supervised features from noise-free seismic data to train blind-spot deconvolution models on contaminated datasets. This approach is demonstrated on a real-world dataset from the North Sea, where it effectively mitigates surface wave interference.

This study examines the influence of charge asymmetry on the scattering of leptons and antileptons off protons, a phenomenon driven by the emission of actual photons. The analysis focuses on the dependence of the differential cross section on the photon's emission angle, utilizing the Yennie-Fermi approximation for this specific angular range. The investigation highlights that the resulting charge asymmetry in the differential cross section arises from the interference between the Coulomb and Breit-Wheeler terms within this approximation. Furthermore, the findings demonstrate that the magnitude of this charge asymmetry is significantly amplified when the scattering angle is small.

The spin-orbit-coupling Mott insulator Sr$_2$IrO$_4$ is a promising candidate for exploring quantum spin liquids. This study employs scanning tunneling spectroscopy to investigate the electronic structure of Sr$_2$IrO$_4$ on the (001) surface. We identify a spin-polaron ladder spectrum characterized by a main peak at 1.1 eV and a secondary peak at 2.1 eV, which aligns well with theoretical predictions. This spectral feature arises from the interplay between strong electron correlations and spin-orbit coupling. Furthermore, we observe a distinct peak at 1.1 eV in the Ir $d_{xy}$ orbital, which is attributed to the in-plane ferromagnetic exchange interaction. These findings provide crucial insights into the magnetic and electronic properties of Sr$_2$IrO$_4$.

Causal mediation analysis seeks to quantify the extent to which a treatment influences an outcome through an intermediate variable. In scenarios involving continuous treatments, prior research has relied on the assumption that all conditional effects are linear to derive closed-form solutions for the doubly robust (DR) estimators of the mediation effect. However, this assumption is often unrealistic, and the resulting linear constraints can lead to biased results. This paper introduces a new method that removes the necessity for such an assumption. By utilizing a weighted two-step estimation approach, we demonstrate that consistent estimation of causal mediation effects is achievable without assuming linearity. Furthermore, we establish the multiple robustness of our proposed estimator, proving that valid results are guaranteed if either the propensity score model or the regression model for the outcome is correctly specified. We also derive the asymptotic distribution of the estimator to facilitate statistical inference. Finally, a simulation study confirms the superior performance of our proposed method compared to existing alternatives.

Suicide prevention is a critical global challenge, with recent research focusing on identifying at-risk individuals through social media content analysis. However, existing datasets are often limited in size, scale, or quality, hindering the development of robust detection systems. To address this, we introduce Robin, an open-access corpus comprising 1.5 million tweets from verified suicide survivors containing suicide-related material. This collection is the most extensive and diverse to date, featuring a balanced representation of gender, age, and race. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of the data, examining the frequency and types of suicidal content, temporal patterns, and the relationship between post severity and user responses. Additionally, we evaluated the performance of current state-of-the-art suicide detection models on Robin, revealing that while these models achieve high accuracy, they suffer from significant false positive rates. These findings underscore the urgent need for novel methodologies to enhance detection accuracy. As an open resource, Robin is available at https://github.com/robin-2021/dataset.

We introduce the concept of blackian mechanics, an information-theoretic framework that examines the dynamics of black holes, specifically regarding their evolution and interactions. This framework relies on the principle of supermanifolds, which unites supermanifolds and bosonization techniques. It establishes a novel approach to analyzing supermanifolds, enabling the construction of superalgebras and supergroups. Furthermore, blackian mechanics facilitates the development of an alternative theory of gravity, which we term (super)Blackian gravity. This theory is grounded in a geometric foundation, where the action functional is derived from the volume of a supermanifold.

This study examines the behavior of solutions for the difference equation $x_{n+1}=a x^\alpha_{n}+b x^\alpha_{n-1}$, where $0<\alpha \leq 2$. We demonstrate that all positive solutions are bounded under specific conditions on the parameters $a$, $b$, and $\alpha$. Furthermore, we prove that the solution sequence converges to an equilibrium point when the parameters satisfy $a+b=1$ and $a>0$.

This study examines a set of generalized Born-Infeld-type models, each defined by a specific function $h(\xi)$, to derive the static, spherically symmetric solutions for charged black holes. The analysis focuses on the properties of the resulting black hole spacetimes, alongside an investigation of the thermodynamics and possible phase transitions. Furthermore, we analyze the geometric attributes of the scalar field and the specific characteristics of the scalar curvature and other curvature invariants.

This work examines the largest possible cardinality of a collection of $d$-tuples from an abelian group that ensures uniqueness in linear combinations with fixed integer coefficients. Specifically, we establish novel upper and lower bounds on this size, which extend known results regarding Sidon sets (where uniqueness applies to pairwise sums with coefficients of 1). Our findings further confirm a conjecture by Pach regarding this problem in the context of finite fields.

We examine the finite-temperature behavior of the magnetic susceptibility and spatial phase in the one-dimensional XY spin chain using the thermodynamic Bethe ansatz. Our findings indicate that the susceptibility displays finite-temperature scaling, a phenomenon that persists even when the system is far from its critical point. Additionally, we observe that the spatial phase transitions from a linear profile at zero temperature to a constant value at high temperatures.

The phase transition of a paramagnetic system into a ferromagnetic state is a critical area of study in condensed matter physics. This work examines the dynamics of this transition using Monte Carlo simulations on 2D and 3D Ising models. We analyze the time-dependent behavior of magnetization and magnetic susceptibility across various temperatures. Our findings indicate that the time evolution of magnetization follows a power law, $M(t) \propto t^{-\alpha}$, where the exponent $\alpha$ decreases as temperature drops. Furthermore, we observe that the magnetization relaxation time, $\tau$, scales with the square of the magnetization itself, expressed as $\tau \propto M^2$.

We examine the localization characteristics of a 1D quasicrystal featuring power-order hopping, defined by $|E_n| \propto n^{-\alpha}$, where $n$ represents the site index. Our findings indicate that for $\alpha < 1$, the system is localized across all energy levels, whereas $\alpha > 1$ yields a mix of localized and delocalized states. Specifically, within the range $1 < \alpha < 2$, an energy gap emerges that separates these states. The states situated above this gap correspond to localized wave functions, while those below it are extended. This work extends prior research on the Fibonacci model, which utilized linear hopping ($|E_n| \propto n$), to scenarios involving power-law decay.

The proliferation of multilingual, task-oriented dialogue systems has heightened the need for Natural Language Processing (NLP) methods capable of bridging linguistic divides. This paper examines multilingual NLP within the context of task-focused dialogues, covering a broad spectrum of challenges ranging from text classification and information retrieval to intent recognition and slot filling. We survey existing multilingual NLP approaches applied to these specific tasks, identifying key limitations and opportunities for future research. Additionally, we outline the prerequisites for developing multilingual models, including the availability of high-quality multilingual data and the integration of transfer learning. We conclude by proposing a potential roadmap for advancing this field.

This study examines the short-term splicing regulation of the *Drosophila melanogaster* *Dscam* gene, which is known to undergo extensive alternative splicing. We analyzed the expression of *Dscam* isoforms in *Drosophila* larval brains using RNA sequencing, revealing that the transcriptome captures only a small fraction of the total isoform diversity. Differential expression of *Dscam* exons was investigated through RNA-seq data, and the results indicate that the expression of alternative exons is not merely binary; rather, it follows a coordinated pattern. We identified two distinct regulatory mechanisms: one where the inclusion of alternative exons inversely correlates with the usage of canonical exons, and another where the inclusion of alternative exons is independent of canonical exon expression levels. These findings suggest that alternative splicing is a dynamic and finely tuned process.

This study investigates how organizations implement technical strategies to safeguard personal data. Drawing on a qualitative analysis of 12 interviews with security and privacy professionals, we identified that while organizations possess a clear understanding of the NIST framework's strategic goals, executing them often proves difficult due to a lack of specific guidance. Our findings reveal that companies frequently encounter obstacles such as balancing security with usability, managing the complexity of data flows, and the high costs associated with security measures. To overcome these challenges, practitioners rely on various internal and external resources, including data maps, privacy impact assessments, and security architecture frameworks. We conclude that the NIST framework should be refined to offer more concrete, technical implementation details, thereby better assisting organizations in achieving privacy and security objectives.

We introduce a novel method for analyzing multiparticle azimuthal correlations in high-energy $pA$ collisions. This approach utilizes the event plane to account for the underlying event background, thereby isolating the genuine short-range correlations between the proton and the nucleus. Our analysis reveals that the $pA$ correlation structure is highly sensitive to the proton's longitudinal momentum fraction, $x$, and that the underlying event significantly distorts these correlations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our technique effectively disentangles the $pA$ correlation function from the event plane, enabling the extraction of the event-plane-independent component. This refined component can be directly compared with theoretical predictions.

The study investigates the production of light nuclei in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=3$ GeV, utilizing a diverse coalescence model that accounts for both quark and hadron-level formation processes. By incorporating hadronization and coalescence mechanisms, the model successfully reproduces the observed kinetic energy per particle and nuclear mass yields. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the mass yields of light nuclei are highly sensitive to the initial collision energy, the chemical freeze-out temperature, and the coalescence radius.

The study of exoplanets has evolved from merely identifying new worlds to investigating their physical characteristics and potential habitability. While the focus on habitability has traditionally centered on the planet's surface conditions, the surrounding environment plays a critical role in determining whether life can exist. This paper reviews the current understanding of planetary environments, specifically addressing how stellar winds, magnetospheres, and radiation belts influence the habitability of terrestrial planets orbiting M-dwarfs. We also examine the effects of extreme stellar flares and orbital tidal forces on potential biospheres. Finally, the review explores the interaction between the planet and its atmosphere, including the potential for atmospheric stripping, and concludes by summarizing the key findings.

This study examines circulant networks, specifically their solubility through a solvable subgroup and a solvable covering group. The paper derives sufficient conditions for determining when circulant networks are solvable, along with sufficient conditions for their solvable coverability.

This paper introduces a novel approach to matrix inversion that leverages iterative techniques, specifically elevating the initial inverse order step-by-step until the precise inverse is attained. The primary contribution is the development of a generalized method capable of raising the order of an existing inverse step by any integer $k \geq 1$, rather than only by one. This advancement enables a more rapid convergence to the exact solution. The authors provide a thorough theoretical foundation for these techniques, alongside a rigorous proof of their validity. Furthermore, the paper outlines a practical algorithm for implementation and demonstrates its efficacy through numerical experiments.

We investigate the impact of back reaction on the power spectrum of primordial curvature perturbations within the framework of ultra-slow-roll (USR) inflation. Our findings indicate that back reaction can significantly alter the amplitude of this spectrum, a modification that becomes especially pronounced during USUR. We demonstrate that the amplitude of the power spectrum is directly proportional to the magnitude of the back reaction coefficient. Furthermore, we analyze the validity of the perturbation theory in the context of USUR inflation and provide a detailed discussion of the associated theoretical implications.

This study introduces a novel formulation termed the Enhanced Selection Optimization (ESO) problem, which extends the classical selection issue by incorporating an additional constraint on the number of selected items. We demonstrate that the ESO problem is NP-hard and subsequently develop an algorithmic framework based on dynamic programming to address it. We analyze the computational complexity of this proposed algorithm and establish a corresponding upper limit for its running time.

The case-base framework serves as an alternative to survival analysis, offering a distinct approach to studying time-to-event data. Unlike traditional survival analysis, which focuses on event frequencies over time, the case-base framework examines event frequencies across different subject groups. This method treats subjects as a shared constant and analyzes how time-specific outcomes vary between groups. By utilizing logistic regression, it incorporates both event and non-event data into its analysis. This paper introduces the case-base framework and demonstrates its application through a simulation study comparing its performance against standard survival analysis techniques.

The advancement of Large Hadron Collider (LHC) demands increasingly precise measurements of Feynman integrals. This necessity has driven the development of sophisticated techniques for evaluating multi-loop integrals, which are essential for achieving the required accuracy levels. This talk provides an overview of the current state of the art in computing multi-loop integrals, with a specific focus on those required for Higgs boson phenomenology.

The increasing adoption of cloud computing has driven a shift toward storing data in cloud environments, where the primary challenge lies in the massive volume of data that must be uploaded and downloaded. This paper evaluates the performance of a data management approach utilizing an object-oriented architecture, specifically comparing the I/O capabilities of the DAOS and Lustre filesystems. The study focuses on the impact of varying block sizes and the number of concurrent threads on overall performance.

The surge in electric vehicle (EV) adoption has spurred the development of EV charging stations, yet these facilities face significant challenges, including long queues and insufficient parking spots. To address this, the proposed digital regulation system manages EV vehicle charging by optimizing the allocation of limited resources. The paper details the design and implementation of this digital regulation mechanism, which prioritizes charging requests based on urgency and energy efficiency. The system's efficacy is validated through a proof-of-concept prototype.

This study examines the occurrence and evolution of locally decodable codes (LCD codes) over finite fields, specifically investigating their minimum distance, the lowest and highest order of regularity, as well as the maximum information rate. We demonstrate that for every finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ and every $d$ where $1 \le d < q$, an LCD code exists achieving minimum distance $d$ and regularity order $d+1$. Furthermore, we establish that LCD codes with $d \ge q-1$ and regularity order $d$ are possible only when $d=q$ and $q$ is a prime number. We also derive an LCD code with regularity order $q-1$ and minimum distance $q-1$ that attains the maximum rate of $1 - \frac{2}{q}$. Finally, we provide a construction of an infinite family of LCD codes with $q$ and regularity order $q$ and minimum distance $q$ and rate $1 - \frac{2}{q}$.

We demonstrate that the one-loop effective potential within a scalar field theory can be reinterpreted as conventional Einstein gravity with an effective Planck mass scaling linearly with the number of scalar fields, $N$. This framework allows us to recover the standard results for the one-loop effective potential derived from the scalar field theory using Einstein's equations. Furthermore, this perspective yields new insights into how the running Planck mass influences the effective gravity scenario.

Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 necessitates a massive transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy, a shift that will inevitably alter land use. This study examines the trade-offs between land use and decarbonization in the Western United States by modeling the expansion of solar and wind capacity alongside the retirement of coal and gas plants. We find that meeting 2050 decarbonization goals requires adding 1.2 to 1.5 times the current land area of the U.S. to host new renewable projects. Furthermore, this transition would likely increase land use by 1.5 to 2.5 times the current area of existing fossil fuel sites. Cluster-randomized trials (CRTs) are frequently employed to evaluate vaccine efficacy. In these studies, entire groups (clusters) of individuals receive either the intervention or control, rather than individuals themselves. This design choice is often driven by ethical, logistical, or practical constraints. However, because CRTs introduce intracluster correlation, they present unique challenges for statistical analysis and interpretation. This article reviews the primary estimands and corresponding statistical methods used in vaccine trials, emphasizing the critical need to align statistical conclusions with the specific research question. We illustrate that the appropriate estimand dictates the necessary statistical approach, and the selected clusters further shape this estimand. Additionally, we examine how the choice of analysis unit—whether at the individual or cluster level—affects the estimand and the resulting conclusions.

The fractionalized standard Laplacian matrix, denoted as $\mathcal{L}_{\alpha}$, is a significant tool in spectral graph theory, with its eigenvalues, $\lambda_k^{\mathcal{L}_{\alpha}}$, defined by the formula $1-\alpha+\lambda_k^{\mathcal{L}}$ for $0 \le \alpha \le 1$. This study examines the spectrum of the fractionalized standard Laplacian matrix for fractal Mobius octagonal networks, denoted as $N_{\mathcal{MO}}(n, \alpha)$, where $n$ represents the order and $\alpha$ is the fractal parameter. We derive both the complete spectrum and the fractal dimension of the network. Furthermore, we analyze how the network's structural parameters influence the spectrum and its associated energy, ultimately deriving the maximum and minimal energy values for $N_{\mathcal{MO}}(n, \alpha)$.

This study examines a distributed online learning scenario where multiple agents operate within a shared, unknown environment. At every time step, a context vector is generated, and each agent receives a specific subset of these vectors. When a context vector is assigned, the agent selects an action and obtains a reward determined by a linear function of an unknown parameter vector and that very context vector. The primary objective is to minimize cumulative regret defined as the difference between the total loss incurred and the loss of the best possible action for every context vector encountered. A critical constraint is that agents do not have access to the full context before selection; they only learn which variables were included in their particular vector after observing the resulting reward. Synthetic data serves as a valuable substitute for real data, particularly in privacy-sensitive contexts like healthcare. Although current techniques can generate realistic data, they often fail to capture the complex interdependencies found in actual records. This paper introduces a novel approach to synthesizing data by modeling the dependencies between attributes, utilizing a two-stage process. First, it employs a Markov model to represent attribute dependencies, followed by a generative adversarial network (GAN) to synthesize data based on that model. We applied this method to create a synthetic cystic fibrosis (CF) patient cohort, demonstrating that the resulting dataset closely mirrors the original real data.

This study examines the $D^{0} \to K^{\mp} \pi^{\pm} \pi^{\pm} \pi^{\mp}$ decay, specifically analyzing the resonance structures within the $\bar{K}^{\mp} \pi^{\pm}$ and $\bar{K}^{\mp} \pi^{\pm} \pi^{\pm}$ invariant mass spectra. The analysis utilizes a data sample of $1.0 \times 10^{9}$ $D^{0}$ mesons collected by the LHCb detector at the LHC. The results indicate that the $\bar{K}^{\mp} \pi^{\pm}$ system is dominated by the $K^{*}(892)^{-}$ resonance, while the $\bar{K}^{\mp} \pi^{\pm} \pi^{\pm}$ system is driven by the $K^{*}(1400)^{-}$ resonance.

Novelpy is a Python library designed to evaluate the originality of scientific publications and patent records by measuring their novelty, disruptiveness, and impact. The tool calculates these metrics by analyzing a document's citation history relative to its citation profile derived from the citation signatures of cited references. The library supports bibliometric datasets from multiple sources, including PubMed, Google Scholar, and the USPTO, as well as various patent databases. Novelpy is built on the SciPy stack and is compatible with the Jupyter Notebook environment.

We introduce a method for generating ultra-short, high-power laser pulses by employing cross-phase modulation (XPM) within a fiber ring cavity. This approach involves a weak, narrowband pump laser interacting with a broadband seed laser in a highly nonlinear fiber. The resulting interaction produces spatiotemporal filtering that autonomously shapes the seed into a pulse with a Gaussian profile in both space and time. Furthermore, the system allows for the generation of high-intensity pulses that can be dynamically controlled by adjusting the pump's polarization. This technique is particularly advantageous for creating ultra-short, high-power pulses in spectral regions where suitable gain media are unavailable.

This paper investigates the potential for robotic systems to master archery using recurve bows. Although the 2021 Tokyo Olympics featured recurve bow as a sport, its complex mechanics—including the bow's asymmetrical draw curve and the necessity for precise arrow release timing—make it a formidable challenge for automation. We begin by developing a physical model of the recurve bow and analyzing the arrow's flight trajectory. Subsequently, we outline a proposed robotic architecture designed to execute this task.

The primary challenge in cross-domain recommendation is bridging the domain gap between source and target domains. While existing methods typically focus on aligning user representations, they often overlook the alignment of item representations, which are equally vital for effective transfer learning. To address this, we introduce Dual Metric Learning (DML), a streamlined yet powerful approach that simultaneously aligns both user and item representations. DML employs a dual-metric learning strategy to enforce user-user similarity and item-item similarity within a shared embedding space. Furthermore, we utilize a user-item cross-metric to capture the inherent structural relationships between users and items. Comprehensive experiments across three real-world datasets demonstrate that DML significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving improvements of 2.9% to 5.1% in Hit Ratio (HitRatio@100) and 2.1% to 4.1% in Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR@100).

We introduce a novel framework for characterizing modal properties of concurrent systems, utilizing distributed automata that operate concurrently. This approach is built upon automata with a specific signature, where the automaton's states are partitioned into distinct teams that run concurrently. This work presents the first formalization of automaton run semantics, along with a new concept of language equivalence for these structures. We demonstrate that the modal mu-segments identified by M. K. Hennessy and M. K. Landy can be characterized as languages accepted by our distributed automata.

This study examines the thermal transfer of intricate charged particles within a two-dimensional plasma characterized by a two-temperature electron distribution. The analysis incorporates the effects of both finite temperature and the influence of the non-local dielectric response. The results demonstrate that the temperature of the electrons significantly impacts the temperature transfer in the system. The study also shows that the transfer of the temperature is influenced by the effects of the non-local dielectric response.
